title: Air
hookLine: every meditation disc is something you can set in front of you. then comes the wind.
tomorrow: do you need deep calm before you can see clearly?

lines: WIND ON A MAP: LITTLE ARROWS.
SO HOW DO YOU GAZE AT THE WIND?
cards: On a weather map, wind is a set of little arrows. Out the window, it's nothing at all. Nobody has ever seen it.
What gets seen is a flag snapping, a plastic bag skating down the street, the top of a tree leaning over. Here's the odd thing. In Buddhaghosa's list of meditation discs, right after fire, sits air.
Earth can be shaped into a disc. Water fits in a bowl. Fire can be framed.
Every one of them is something you can set in front of you and look at. So how do you gaze at the wind?

teach.b: His answer: you don't look at the wind.
You look at what it moves, or you feel where it lands. By sight, you watch the tops of tall plants swaying, sugarcane or bamboo, or a tree, or even the loose ends of someone's hair.
And the mind notes it plainly: this wind is striking this place. By touch, you sit where wind comes through a window or a crack in a wall, and feel it on your skin, with the same plain note.
The name to hold is vayo, air, or vata, wind. So the puzzle solves itself in an interesting way.

teach.h: IT SHOWS UP AS A MEETING.
teach.b: The wind is real, but it only ever shows up as a meeting: air and leaf, air and cheek.

Then the stages, as with fire. At first the sign moves, and his picture for it is homey: like heat shimmering off a pot of rice porridge just taken from the stove. Later a steadier sign comes, quiet and still.
The meditator never chases the wind. He sits where it already blows. A lot of what matters works like that: a kindness, a mood in a room, a good influence.
Nobody sees them directly. You see what they move.

how: In Theravada meditation manuals the air kasina is taken up by sight, watching plant tops or hair move in the wind, or by touch, feeling wind on the body, as the Visuddhimagga describes; it is practiced with a teacher's guidance.

o: wind, known by what it moves and where it touches
an empty sky, imagined with no clouds in it
the breath, counted slowly to calm a busy mind

games.q: how you catch the wind — tap the pairs.
p: wind on skin through a window

s: you have to see something to meditate on it
the air practice can be done by touch: wind on the skin, through a window or a crack in a wall.
the air practice is a breathing exercise
it watches outside wind: plant tops swaying, or wind on skin. breathing is a separate subject.
Buddhaghosa likens the moving sign to heat shimmering off rice porridge
the steadier sign that follows is quiet and still.

games.q: your little cousin says kindness isn't real, because you can't see it. what would the air practice say back?
o: fair point: if you can't see it, it's only a nice idea.
you see it the way you see wind: in what it moves.
it's only real once someone measures it properly.
games.why: nobody sees wind directly. the practice watches what it moves and feels where it lands, and that's enough to know it's there.

practice: Find a window, a doorway or a fan, anything stirring the air near you. Watch one thing it moves, a leaf, a curtain, a strand of hair, and then feel the air arrive on your face or hands. Each time, note it plainly: wind, here.

wordCard.voice: Air: vayo in Pali. Known by what it moves and where it touches, never seen on its own.

orig.note: Pali: air, the moving element. The name held in mind while watching what the wind moves.

carryVoice: Something to keep: the moving wind, never seen itself, only in the leaves it moves. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 5 (the air kasina: taken by sight, the tops of sugarcane, bamboo or trees, or the ends of hair moving in the wind; or by touch, wind striking the body through a window or a crack in a wall; 'this wind is striking this place'; the names vata/vayo; the learning sign moving like heat from rice gruel just off the oven, the counterpart sign quiet and motionless)
